title: How the “censorship-industrial complex” is changing the Internet and US policy
raw_text: I first heard the term “censorship-industrial complex” on April 15, 2025. That’s when I got the tip that a small office in the U.S. State Department, which focused on monitoring and countering foreign disinformation from the likes of Russia, Iran, and China, was facing imminent shutdown—the next day. And the reason? R/FIMI, as the office was called, was accused of serving as the State Department’s central hub in the so-called censorship-industrial complex—a sprawling constellation of government agencies, academics, civil society groups, and Big Tech platforms allegedly conspiring to suppress conservative and populist speech online under the guise of combating disinformation. I broke the story around 10:30AM on April 16, (and broke more in the weeks that followed) but for me, it was just the start of a deep reporting rabbit-hole into an idea that had moved from the fringes of the right-wing Internet into the mainstream, championed and spread by a network of well-funded conservative media platforms and non-profits, and finally as a sort of prevailing logic behind much of the second Trump administration’s domestic and foreign policy. But this isn’t just a policy story. The weaponization of ideas about censorship also affects the billions of people globally who get information, or interact with each other, online—which is to say, all of us. For more on what the narrative means for the Internet, read my story here .

title: AI professors are negotiating the new realities of academic research
raw_text: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . Last week, I headed 30 miles south of San Francisco to a hotel in Mountain View, California, to join some of the most accomplished, and some of the most promising, AI researchers in the world. I was hosting roundtable interviews and speaking at a media training for a convening of the Schmidt Sciences AI2050 program, an initiative funded by Eric and Wendy Schmidt that supports academics whose work involves AI. The fellows list is a who’s who of AI luminaries, and though not all of them made it out to the Bay, every time I turned a corner I saw a scientist whom I’d interviewed previously or whose research I admired. (Full disclosure: I received a science communication award funded by Schmidt Sciences in 2024.) It’s a weird time for university AI researchers, who make up most of the AI2050 group. In the past four years, AI research has reoriented around large language models, and its cutting edge has moved from academic institutions to private companies. Universities simply can’t afford the GPUs required to train and run frontier models, and even if they could, Anthropic and OpenAI aren’t letting anyone else see the inner details of Claude or ChatGPT. title: The Download: AI agents for science, and the “censorship-industrial complex”
raw_text: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. AI for science needs reasoning, not just data —Eric Schmidt, the former CEO of Google and the cofounder of Schmidt Sciences, and Suhas Mahesh, who leads the AI for science work at the AI Center of Schmidt Sciences In 2024, Google DeepMind scientists shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for a neural network, AlphaFold, which predicts the structures of proteins. It showed that AI could make groundbreaking scientific discoveries, but AlphaFold may not be the best template for accelerating science. Instead, another approach may hold the key: AI agents. AlphaFold relied on a dataset of roughly 170,000 experimentally validated protein structures that took 53 years and roughly $21 billion worth of experimental work to assemble. Comparable datasets will be difficult or impossible to create in many fields. AI agents can instead model the iterative, highly contingent process of actual research. While tools like AlphaFold apply a powerful approach to a limited question, agents are inherently generalists. They do not represent a new way to do science—instead, they digitally model the human process of discovery. Read the full op-ed on how agents could accelerate scientific discovery . raw_text: From the Arkansas Advocate: Arkansas library directors said they have several unanswered questions about how a 2023 state law restricting access to library materials will be enforced after a federal appeals court ruled that it can go into effect. title: AI for science needs reasoning, not just data
raw_text: Every few decades, someone announces that science has reached its end. In 1903, the revered physicist Albert Michelson wrote that the “facts of physical science have all been discovered.” In the 1980s, Stephen Hawking predicted that theoretical physics might be finished by the end of the century. With the explosive arrival of artificial intelligence, the feeling is in the air again—this time accompanied by a Nobel Prize. In 2024, Demis Hassabis and John Jumper of Google DeepMind were awarded part of the Nobel in chemistry for their neural network AlphaFold, which predicts the three-dimensional structures of proteins by learning from thousands of experimentally measured shapes. This devilish problem had resisted systematic attacks for half a century; AlphaFold seemed to have solved it once and for all, and the world became fixated on the promise of its approach. Hassabis and his team called AlphaFold “the template for how AI can accelerate all of science to digital speed.” A wave of startups building foundation models for biology, chemistry, and materials discovery raised billions of dollars, buoyed by DeepMind’s success. AlphaFold had shown that the combination of AI and sufficient data could make groundbreaking discoveries (even if we did not understand the underlying mechanisms involved), and it seemed, once again, that a path through the rest of science was laid out before us. title: These startups are chasing the next big thing in LLMs
raw_text: MIT Technology Review ’s What’s Next series looks across industries, trends, and technologies to give you a first look at the future. You can read the rest of them here . Way back in the summer of 2017, AI researchers at Google put out a paper called “Attention Is All You Need,” in which they described a new type of neural network called a transformer. It proved to be very good at processing long sequences of data, especially text. Nine years on, transformers are the engines inside every major large language model on the market. “The entire AI industry is built on transformers,” says Justin Dangel, cofounder and CEO of the AI startup Subquadratic. “They are one of the most important innovations in the history of computer science, and they’ve changed the world.” But transformers are starting to show their age. Many of the recent advances in LLMs, such as the development of so-called reasoning models and their ability to handle large amounts of input at once, are not neat extensions of that core technology but workarounds that patch over some of its fundamental flaws. A growing number of scientists and engineers are now asking what’s coming next. LLMs are not going anywhere, but the way they get built is up for grabs. ( MIT Technology Review dubbed this future generation of models LLMs+ in this year’s list of the 10 things that matter in AI .) On June 12, 2026, Anthropic suspended access to both models to comply with U.S. Department of Commerce export controls; the Department lifted those controls on June 30, 2026, and Anthropic restored access on July 1, 2026 (Anthropic's statement: https://www.anthropic.com/news/fable-mythos-access ). title: GitHub Models is now retired
raw_text: GitHub Models is now retired I missed this news until today, when the GitHub Actions run for my simonw/research repository failed with this error message: GitHub Models is temporarily unavailable as part of a scheduled retirement brownout. That message is already stale, because the retirement has been completed. GitHub Models was an odd-shaped duck. GitHub provided a model playground tool and a unified API across a bunch of different LLM providers, with the biggest benefit being that code running in GitHub Actions could use the GitHub API key already present in that environment to execute prompts. This made it easy to build things that fit GitHub Next's Continuous AI concept. GitHub didn't share the reason behind the shutdown, but my bet is that it fits the pattern where coding agent patterns made it prohibitively expensive to offer free or subsidized tokens. My workflow uses an LLM call to create folder summaries for the README , using this code here . I swapped GitHub Models out for an OpenAI API key with a monthly spending limit, and I'm now generating my summaries using GPT-5.6 Luna. title: International research and library collaboration: concern for the future, but action possible!
raw_text: Libraries are contributing to international research collaborations, as well as engaging themselves in regular cross-border cooperation. Yet a significant share frequently encounter barriers that prevent them from working together, or create frustration or uncertainty. There is scope to do more, both through our professional and advocacy work. At international level, there is a growing focus on the need to support and enable collaboration between researchers in different countries. This is driven both by the scale and seriousness of global challenges that require scientific responses, and by the concern that such collaboration is only getting harder at a time of polarisation. From the International Science Council’s work on research and innovation cooperation to the European Union’s recent highlighting of the need to boost science diplomacy , there is recognition that working together is valuable, but also under threat. Libraries have an important role to play in such collaborations, given their existing vital contribution as a key research infrastructure. Enabling access to knowledge is a central part of collaboration, both through sharing materials with researchers and institutions remotely, and welcoming visitors. As managers of data and other repositories, they also support the dissemination of the results of collaboration. Laboratory courses provide authentic contexts for undergraduate students to learn data curation skills. We evaluated a curriculum-integrated, librarian-led module in a senior biomedical engineering laboratory course that demonstrated strategies for using generative AI for RDM tasks and included practice exercises that guided students through using AI to assist with data cleaning and data processing. Students completed identical pre/post surveys, which included four open-response questions and three Likert-scale questions. title: IFLA-GOVLIB collaborates on the State Level Seminar on public libraries in Kota, India
raw_text: The IFLA Government Libraries Section (GOVLIB) is pleased to join as an international collaborator in the State Level Seminar on Public Libraries and Librarians (SLS–PLLSCD 2026). Under the title ‘ Public Libraries and Librarians: Making a Difference to Society and Cultural Development’ , the event will be held on 12 August 2026 at the Government Divisional Public Library in Kota, Rajasthan, India. The date marks National Librarians’ Day and the birth anniversary of Padma Shri Dr S. R. Ranganathan , one of the founding figures of modern library science. Organised by the Department of Language and Library, Government of Rajasthan , the event brings together more than ten expert sessions alongside nine peer-reviewed research papers. Topics range from artificial intelligence in public libraries and inclusive technologies to library automation, the Right to Information Act, Indian Knowledge Systems, and the enduring relevance of Ranganathan’s Five Laws in the age of agentic AI. The day closes with a panel discussion on how AI is transforming public library services and communities. Among the event’s partners are the Raja Rammohun Roy Library Foundation, XLRI Xavier School of Management, and universities in Nigeria. The seminar is convened by Dr Deepak Kumar Shrivastava , Divisional Librarian and Head of the Government Divisional Public Library, Kota, and a member of the GOVLIB Standing Committee.

raw_text: From Hartford Business: One of the world’s largest collections of recorded music has found a permanent home in Connecticut. The Archive of Contemporary Music , a nonprofit repository of more than 3 million sound recordings that was forced out of New York City by soaring rents, has purchased a commercial building in Ridgefield where it plans to open a public archive and cultural destination by 2028. [Clip] Founded in 1985, ARC bills itself as America’s largest archive dedicated to popular music and contemporary recorded sound. Its holdings span more than 3,000 musical genres and include more than 3 million recordings, along with thousands of photographs, books, magazines, videos, sheet music and other artifacts documenting recorded music since 1945. The purchase ends a yearslong search for a permanent home. Co-founder and Director B. George launched ARC in a lower Manhattan loft before the organization settled in Tribeca, where it remained until 2020. Rising rents and limited space forced the archive to close its longtime New York location, and the collection has since been housed in a storage facility in Dutchess County donated by hotelier André Balazs. title: IFLA-GOVLIB’s Collaboration for I-LIPS 2026: Strengthening Regional Networking and Connections
raw_text: The IFLA Government Libraries Section (GOVLIB) is proud to join the 14th International Library and Information Professionals Summit (I-LIPS 2026) as an international collaborator. The summit will be hosted by University of Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh, India from 30th October to 01st November. This year’s event, under the title “Empowering Indian Knowledge Systems through National Education Policy, Artificial Intelligence and Sustainable Libraries for Viksit Bharat 2047” will explore the intersection of artificial intelligence, national education policy, sustainable libraries, libraries as pillars of the knowledge economy for Viksit Bharat 2047, and Indian knowledge systems, bringing together professionals and researchers to exchange ideas and showcase innovative practices. Regional partnerships and collaborations play a vital role in strengthening IFLA’s goal for the global library community. IFLA-GOVLIB is delighted to contribute to an international conference that encourages dialogue, collaboration and the sharing of knowledge, resources and networks across countries. The Summit is open to academicians, library professionals, researchers, scholars and practitioners from around the world. Those wishing to contribute and participate can submit abstracts until 31 July 2026, with registration remaining open until 15 October 2026 . Further information on participation, submissions and the programme is available on the conference website: https://www.ilips2026.in

title: IFLA 100: The History and Strategic Role of the Management of Library Associations Section (MLAS)
raw_text: In celebration of IFLA’s 100 and aligned with our IFLA President “Be Bold” theme, the IFLA Management of Library Associations Section is pleased to share the following paper, now available on the IFLA Repository : “The History and Strategic Role of the Management of Library Associations Section (MLAS): Building Strong Library Associations in an Era of Global – Transformation An Institutional History of MLAS, 1983–2026” Abstract This paper presents an institutional history of IFLA’s Management of Library Associations Section (MLAS) . Tracing its evolution from the Round Table for the Management of Library Associations (RTMLA), established in 1983, to its current role in strengthening library associations worldwide. It examines key milestones, including the transition from RTMLA to an IFLA Section in 2002, the recognition of library association representation within IFLA governance, its commitment to developing the next generation of library leaders through its sponsorship of the IFLA New Professionals Special Interest Group (NPSIG ), and the expansion of MLAS’s work in leadership development, capacity building, advocacy, mentoring, and international collaboration. title: All About Heritage Adapts! for Libraries: Recording available
raw_text: Climate change is the defining issue of our time, and among the greatest threats facing cultural and natural heritage today. We know libraries have limited bandwidth, resources, support, and connections to plan for and adapt to the effects of a changing climate. That is why IFLA wants to help our members build resilience – protecting libraries, collections and community spaces that are so important for helping our communities adapt. What does Heritage Adapts! mean for libraries? We invited members and volunteers to join us in a live information and Q&A Session to learn more about the initiative, what it could mean for their work, and how they can join. A Global Campaign IFLA is proud to join partners in Heritage Adapts! Launched in June 2026, this is the first global campaign uniting the heritage sector behind a shared mission: at least 3,000 sites and practices taking locally led climate adaptation action by 2030. Recognized under the U.N.’s Global Climate Action Agenda as one of 120 promising climate delivery plans, Heritage Adapts! demonstrates how protecting heritage (including libraries!) can strengthen community resilience. Find out more here. We are excited to invite you to join us in this mission! Find out more about Heritage Adapts! and start adapting at act.heritageadapts.org Contact claire.mcguire@ifla.org with questions.

title: World Book Capital 2028: Call for Applications Open
raw_text: Cities and towns with a great story to tell – and great plans ahead – about placing books and reading at the heart of their urban development are encouraged to consider appying to be UNESCO World Book Capital City 2028. Deadline: 7 October. UNESCO’s World Book Capital programme celebrates places that recgonise and mobilise the potential of proting books, reading, literacy and access to knowledge in order to improve the lives of their inhabitants and communities. The 28th holder of this title will join a group of cities around the world that have demonstated how investing and innovating in reading and writing, as well as the libraries, publishers and bookshops that support them, can make a difference. Winning cities typically have a strong engagement of libraries at the heart of their bids, alongside that of publishing houses, writers organisations and bookshops. As such, IFLA sits alongside the International Publishers Association, the International Authors Forum, and the European and International Booksellers’ Federation and UNESO on the Advisory Committee for this. The final decision is taken by the UNESCO Director General. The holder of the 2027 title – Medellín, Colombia , already demonstrates a very strong integration of libraries in its bid, building on its history as the home of the UNESCO Pilot Public Library.
